name: Eye yoga / eye exercises
lead: Eye yoga, or eye exercises, refers to routines of deliberate eye movements, palming, focus shifting and relaxation that practitioners say can relieve strain, improve vision and, in looksmaxxing circles, firm or brighten the skin around the eyes. The practice draws on a lineage that includes the Bates method, an alternative therapy developed by the American eye doctor William Horatio Bates (1860-1931).[1]

Reviews of the vision-training literature have not found objective evidence that eye exercises improve eyesight; an American Academy of Ophthalmology review and a 2005 review of 43 studies reported no clear benefit for visual acuity.[1] No published study found in the sources reviewed has tested eye exercises for the appearance of the skin or tissues around the eyes.

paras: Techniques associated with the Bates method include palming (covering closed eyes with the palms without pressure), visualising small black letters or dots, and shifting or swinging the gaze.[1] Modern "eye yoga" routines commonly combine such techniques with rolling or focusing exercises.

Bates reported in 1891 that he had reversed several cases of myopia, and in 1920 he self-published Perfect Sight Without Glasses.[1] In 1917 he partnered with Bernarr Macfadden on a correspondence course that the American Medical Association criticised, and in 1929 the US Federal Trade Commission filed a complaint over misleading advertising.[1] Aldous Huxley popularised the approach in The Art of Seeing (1942).[1]

Laboratory measurements published in 1998 found that the eyeball changes length only minutely during focusing, far less than the Bates theory required.[1] The American Academy of Ophthalmology review found no evidence that visual training objectively improves eyesight, and attributed reported gains to factors such as better interpretation of blurred images, mood or the pinhole effect of the pupil.[1]

Commentators on the Bates method note that sungazing can injure the eye, pressing on the eyeballs while palming may raise glaucoma risk, and abandoning corrective lenses can be unsafe or delay treatment of conditions such as glaucoma or amblyopia.[1]
No studies found for eye exercises as a treatment for the appearance of the eye area. Studies of vision training for visual acuity, reviewed in the Bates method literature, found no clear benefit.[1]

timeline.event: Bates reports reversing cases of myopia.[1]
Huxley publishes The Art of Seeing.[1]
Review of 43 studies finds no clear evidence that eye exercises improve acuity.[1]

card.summary: Eye movement and relaxation routines claimed to firm the eye area; no studies support an appearance effect.
card.note: Related Bates-method practices such as sungazing carry documented risks.

quick.overview:
Eye yoga is a set of eye-movement and relaxation routines. Some in looksmaxxing circles say it firms or brightens the eye area.

No studies were found testing this. Reviews of eye exercises for vision itself found no clear benefit.
quick.mechanism: Practitioners move or rest the eyes through set routines, on the theory that this relieves strain or tone in the surrounding muscles.
quick.risks: Plain eye movements are low-risk, but related Bates-method practices like sungazing or pressing on the eyes have documented risks, and abandoning glasses can be unsafe.
